title: Canopy Uniformity, Flower Position and Corrective Strategy

content.overview: Uniformity is not visual flatness. Useful canopy uniformity evaluates whether flower sites experience comparable light, airflow and developmental opportunity and whether resulting biomass/chemistry differences are acceptable for the production goal.

vocabulary.definition: Similarity of a measured condition across defined canopy locations.
Location of an inflorescence within the plant/canopy, including height and interior/edge context.
A targeted change selected to address a measured source of nonuniformity.

sections.title: Map cause before correction
sections.body: A low-performing interior zone can arise from shading, airflow, irrigation, architecture or multiple interacting factors. Measure before choosing pruning or lighting changes.

sections.title: Architecture and chemistry can covary
sections.body: Cannabis research has shown architecture can influence chemical uniformity across large plants.

sections.title: Corrective tools have tradeoffs
sections.body: Spacing, trellising, pruning and interlighting can improve distribution while changing labor, heat load and plant stress. Compare benefit against system cost.

workedExamples: Lower-canopy quality variation caused mainly by low PPFD may not be fixed by simply increasing air movement.
A flat trellis top can still hide dense internal shading.
commonMistakes: Judging uniformity only by canopy height.
Changing pruning and lighting simultaneously without a baseline.
Ignoring flower-position data when comparing quality.
content.practicalApplication: Select representative flower positions, map light/environment and compare harvest/quality measurements by position before choosing one corrective factor.
content.summary: Canopy uniformity becomes actionable when spatial measurements are connected to flower outcomes and targeted corrections.
